stem: Which one of the following materials cannot be used to make a lens?
solution:
A lens works by **refracting light that passes through it**, so the material must be **transparent**.

- (A) **Water**, (B) **glass** and (C) **plastic** are all transparent — light passes through and is refracted, so each can make a lens.
- **(D) Clay is opaque.** No light passes through it at all, so there is nothing to refract and it cannot make a lens.

Water genuinely works, awkward though it sounds: a water-filled container of the right shape behaves as a lens.
groundedIn: §9.3 Refraction of Light and §9.3.3 Refraction by Spherical Lenses, which describe a lens as a transparent material bound by two surfaces through which light passes and is refracted.

stem: The image formed by a concave mirror is observed to be virtual, erect and larger than the object. Where should be the position of the object?

options.label: A
options.text: Between the principal focus and the centre of curvature

options.label: D
options.text: Between the pole of the mirror and its principal focus

solution:
A concave mirror gives a **virtual** image in exactly one case, and that fixes the answer — **(D), between the pole and the principal focus**. There the image is virtual, erect and enlarged, and it cannot be caught on a screen; it has to be looked for in the mirror itself.

Every other option gives a **real, inverted** image:

- (A) Between F and C → beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged.
- (B) At C → at C, real, inverted, same size.
- (C) Beyond C → between F and C, real, inverted, diminished.

This position is the one used for a **shaving mirror** and by **dentists**.
groundedIn: §9.2.1 Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors with Activity 9.3 and Table 9.1, which tabulate the nature, position and relative size of the image for every object position from infinity to between P and F.

stem: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get a real image of the size of the object?

options.label: A
options.text: At the principal focus of the lens

options.label: D
options.text: Between the optical centre of the lens and its principal focus

solution:
**(B) At twice the focal length**, that is at \(2F_1\). The image then forms at \(2F_2\) on the other side and is **real, inverted and the same size** as the object.

Checking it with the lens formula for \(u = -2f\):

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{-2f} = \dfrac{1}{2f}\), so \(v = 2f\) and \(m = v/u = -1\) — inverted, same size.

- (A) At the principal focus → the image is at **infinity**, highly magnified.
- (C) At infinity → the image is at the focus, a point-sized real image.
- (D) Between the optical centre and F → the image is **virtual**, erect and enlarged.
groundedIn: §9.3.4 Image Formation by Lenses with Table 9.4, which gives the nature, position and size of the image formed by a convex lens for each object position, and §9.3.7 for the lens formula.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: A spherical mirror and a thin spherical lens have each a focal length of –15 cm. The mirror and the lens are likely to be

options.label: C
options.text: the mirror is concave and the lens is convex

options.label: D
options.text: the mirror is convex, but the lens is concave

solution:
Read the **sign** through the New Cartesian convention for each device separately.

- For a **mirror**, a negative focal length means the principal focus lies **in front of** the mirror — which is the case for a **concave** mirror.
- For a **lens**, a negative focal length means the lens is **diverging** — which is a **concave** lens.

Both are therefore concave, so **(A)**.

It is worth noticing that the same sign means two different geometrical facts here: for the mirror it places the focus on the object side, for the lens it makes the rays diverge. They agree in this case, but they are not the same rule.
groundedIn: §9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors and §9.3.6 Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses, which fix the sign of the focal length for concave and convex mirrors and for converging and diverging lenses.

stem: No matter how far you stand from a mirror, your image appears erect. The mirror is likely to be
solution:
The words **“no matter how far”** are doing the work: the mirror must give an erect image for **every** object distance.

- A **plane** mirror always gives a virtual, erect image of the same size. ✓
- A **convex** mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image, whatever the distance. ✓
- A **concave** mirror gives an erect image **only** when the object is between the pole and the principal focus; move further away and the image becomes real and inverted. ✗

So two of the three mirrors qualify, which rules out (A) and (C) — each excludes a mirror that also works — and (B) outright. The answer is **(D) either plane or convex**.
groundedIn: §9.2.1 Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors with Table 9.1 and Table 9.2, which give the concave mirror's image as erect only for an object between P and F and the convex mirror's as always virtual and erect.

stem: Which of the following lenses would you prefer to use while reading small letters found in a dictionary?

options.label: A
options.text: A convex lens of focal length 50 cm

options.label: B
options.text: A concave lens of focal length 50 cm

options.label: C
options.text: A convex lens of focal length 5 cm

options.label: D
options.text: A concave lens of focal length 5 cm

solution:
Reading small letters needs a **magnifying glass**, and that means two things at once.

**1. The lens must be convex.** Only a convex lens can give a virtual, erect and **enlarged** image, with the object held between the optical centre and the focus. A **concave** lens always gives a **diminished** image, so (B) and (D) are out however short their focal length.

**2. The focal length should be short.** The shorter \(f\) is, the greater the power \(P = 1/f\) and the greater the magnification. A 5 cm lens has \(P = +20\) D against \(+2\) D for a 50 cm lens.

So **(C), a convex lens of focal length 5 cm**.
groundedIn: §9.3.4 Image Formation by Lenses with Table 9.4, for the virtual, erect, enlarged image from a convex lens with the object between O and F, and §9.3.8 Power of a Lens for \(P = 1/f\).

stem: We wish to obtain an erect image of an object, using a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. What should be the range of distance of the object from the mirror? What is the nature of the image? Is the image larger or smaller than the object? Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation in this case.
solution:
**Range of object distance.** A concave mirror gives an **erect** image only when the object lies **between the pole and the principal focus**. With \(f = 15\) cm, that means

**any distance less than 15 cm** from the mirror — that is, \(0 < \text{object distance} < 15\) cm.

**Nature of the image.** **Virtual and erect.** It is formed **behind the mirror**, so it cannot be caught on a screen and must be looked for in the mirror itself.

**Size.** **Larger than the object** — the image is enlarged. This is the arrangement used in a shaving mirror and by dentists.

**Ray diagram.** Place the object AB between P and F. Draw two rays from the top of the object:

- One **parallel to the principal axis**, which after reflection passes through F.
- One **directed towards the centre of curvature C**, which returns along its own path.

The reflected rays **diverge** and do not meet in front of the mirror. Extend them **backwards** as dotted lines; they appear to meet behind the mirror, and that is where the enlarged, erect, virtual image forms.
groundedIn: §9.2.1 Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors with Activity 9.3, Table 9.1 and Fig. 9.7, which give the virtual, erect, enlarged image for an object between P and F and the standard rays used to locate it.

context: Name the type of mirror used in the following situations. Support your answer with reason.
solution:
**A concave mirror.**

**Reason.** The bulb is placed at the **principal focus** of the mirror. Rays that leave a source at the focus are reflected **parallel to the principal axis**, so the headlight sends out a **powerful parallel beam** of light that travels a long distance without spreading.

A convex mirror would diverge the light and illuminate almost nothing.
groundedIn: §9.2.2, under Uses of concave mirrors, which states that concave mirrors are commonly used in torches, search-lights and vehicle headlights to get powerful parallel beams of light.

context: Name the type of mirror used in the following situations. Support your answer with reason.
solution:
**A convex mirror.**

**Reason.** Two properties matter here:

- It always gives an **erect, though diminished, image**, whatever the distance of the vehicle behind.
- Being **curved outwards**, it has a **wider field of view**, so the driver can see a much larger area behind than a plane mirror of the same size would show.
groundedIn: §9.2.2, under Uses of convex mirrors, which gives both the always-erect diminished image and the wider field of view from the outward curve.

context: Name the type of mirror used in the following situations. Support your answer with reason.
solution:
**A concave mirror** — a large one.

**Reason.** A concave mirror **converges** the parallel rays arriving from the Sun to its **principal focus**. Concentrating all that sunlight into one small spot produces a very high temperature there, which is exactly what a solar furnace needs.

Activity 9.2 is the same effect in miniature: sunlight focused by a concave mirror onto a sheet of paper makes it smoke and eventually catch fire.
groundedIn: §9.2.2, under Uses of concave mirrors, which states that large concave mirrors are used to concentrate sunlight to produce heat in solar furnaces, with Activity 9.2 for the burning paper.

stem: One-half of a convex lens is covered with a black paper. Will this lens produce a complete image of the object? Verify your answer experimentally. Explain your observations.
solution:
**Yes — the lens will still produce a complete image of the object.**

**Why.** Every point of the object sends out rays that strike **the whole surface** of the lens, and each of those rays is refracted to the same image point. Covering half the lens only blocks **some** of those rays; the ones passing through the uncovered half still come together at the same place and form the **whole** image.

What changes is not the shape of the image but its **brightness**: with fewer rays reaching it, the image is **fainter** than before.

**Experimental verification.**

- Place a lighted candle in front of a convex lens and obtain a sharp image on a screen. Note its shape, size and brightness.
- Now cover the **upper** half of the lens with black paper. The image is still complete, but dimmer.
- Repeat with the **lower** half covered. The result is the same.

**Observation.** In every case the image is complete and of the same size and position; only its intensity falls. This is what confirms that no single part of a lens is responsible for any particular part of the image.
groundedIn: §9.3.4 Image Formation by Lenses and §9.3.5 Image Formation in Lenses Using Ray Diagrams with Fig. 9.16, where the image point is located as the meeting point of rays refracted through different parts of the lens.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: An object 5 cm in length is held 25 cm away from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Draw the ray diagram and find the position, size and the nature of the image formed.
solution:
**Given.** \(h = +5\) cm, \(u = -25\) cm, \(f = +10\) cm (converging).

**Position.**

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{-25} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{50} = \dfrac{3}{50}\)

\(v = \dfrac{50}{3} = +16.7\) cm

The image is **16.7 cm from the lens, on the side opposite the object**.

**Size.**

\(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{50/3}{-25} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\)

\(h' = m\,h = -\dfrac{2}{3} \times 5 = -3.3\) cm

**Nature.** The positive \(v\) makes the image **real**; the negative \(h'\) makes it **inverted**; and \(|m| < 1\) makes it **diminished** — 3.3 cm against an object of 5 cm.

**Ray diagram.** The object at 25 cm lies **beyond \(2F_1\)** (which is at 20 cm), so the image forms between \(F_2\) and \(2F_2\) on the other side. Draw one ray parallel to the axis, refracted through \(F_2\), and one through the optical centre, which goes straight on; they meet at the top of the inverted image.
groundedIn: §9.3.7 Lens Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = v/u\), with §9.3.6 Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: A concave lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image 10 cm from the lens. How far is the object placed from the lens? Draw the ray diagram.
solution:
**Given.** \(f = -15\) cm (concave). A concave lens always forms a **virtual, erect image on the same side as the object**, so the image distance is negative: \(v = -10\) cm.

**Object position.**

\(\dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-10} - \dfrac{1}{-15} = \dfrac{-3 + 2}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{30}\)

\(u = -30\) cm

**The object is placed 30 cm from the lens.**

**Ray diagram.** Draw the concave lens with the object AB at 30 cm on the left. From the top of the object:

- One ray **parallel to the principal axis**, which after refraction **appears to diverge from \(F_1\)** on the object's side.
- One ray through the **optical centre**, which passes straight through.

The two emergent rays diverge. Extending them **backwards** as dotted lines, they appear to meet 10 cm from the lens on the object's side — giving a **virtual, erect, diminished** image there.

Getting the sign of \(v\) from the physics rather than from the words “10 cm from the lens” is the whole of this question.
groundedIn: §9.3.7 Lens Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = v/u\), with §9.3.6 Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses.

stem: An object is placed at a distance of 10 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
solution:
**Given.** \(u = -10\) cm, \(f = +15\) cm (convex, so the focus is behind the mirror).

**Position.**

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{-10} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2 + 3}{30} = \dfrac{5}{30}\)

\(v = +6.0\) cm

The positive sign puts the image **6.0 cm behind the mirror**.

**Nature.**

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{6.0}{-10} = +0.6\)

The image is **virtual** (it is behind the mirror), **erect** (the positive \(m\)) and **diminished** (\(|m| < 1\), 0.6 times the object's size).

All three conclusions were fixed in advance by the mirror being convex — a convex mirror gives nothing else, whatever the object distance.
groundedIn: §9.2.4 Mirror Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v + 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = -v/u\), with §9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors for the New Cartesian signs.

stem: The magnification produced by a plane mirror is +1. What does this mean?
solution:
It carries two separate pieces of information, one in the magnitude and one in the sign.

**The magnitude, 1.** Magnification is \(m = h'/h\), so \(|m| = 1\) means the **image is exactly the same size as the object** — neither enlarged nor diminished.

**The positive sign.** A positive magnification means the image is **virtual and erect**. (A negative value would mean a real, inverted image.)

Together: a plane mirror forms an image of the **same size as the object, virtual and erect** — which is exactly what we see in an ordinary mirror.
groundedIn: §9.2.4 Mirror Formula and Magnification, which defines \(m = h'/h = -v/u\) and fixes the meaning of its sign and magnitude.

stem: An object 5.0 cm in length is placed at a distance of 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm. Find the position of the image, its nature and size.
solution:
**Given.** \(h = +5.0\) cm, \(u = -20\) cm, \(R = +30\) cm (convex).

**Focal length.**

\(f = \dfrac{R}{2} = +15\) cm

**Position.**

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{4 + 3}{60} = \dfrac{7}{60}\)

\(v = \dfrac{60}{7} = +8.6\) cm

The image is **8.6 cm behind the mirror**.

**Nature and size.**

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{60/7}{-20} = \dfrac{3}{7} = +0.43\)

\(h' = m\,h = \dfrac{3}{7} \times 5.0 = \dfrac{15}{7} = 2.1\) cm

The image is **virtual, erect and diminished** — about 2.1 cm tall against an object of 5.0 cm.

**A note on the rounding.** The exact image height is \(15/7 = 2.14\) cm. Some answer keys give 2.2 cm, which comes from rounding \(v\) to 8.6 cm **first** and then computing \(m = 0.43\) and \(h' = 0.43 \times 5.0 = 2.15\). Both describe the same image; carrying the exact fraction through to the end gives 2.1 cm.
groundedIn: §9.2.4 Mirror Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v + 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = -v/u\), with §9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors for the New Cartesian signs.

stem: An object of size 7.0 cm is placed at 27 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 18 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed, so that a sharp focussed image can be obtained? Find the size and the nature of the image.
solution:
**Given.** \(h = +7.0\) cm, \(u = -27\) cm, \(f = -18\) cm (concave).

**Position of the screen.**

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{-18} - \dfrac{1}{-27} = \dfrac{-3 + 2}{54} = -\dfrac{1}{54}\)

\(v = -54\) cm

The negative sign places the image **in front of the mirror, on the object's side**, so the **screen should be placed 54 cm from the mirror**. An image that can be caught on a screen is **real**.

**Size.**

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-54}{-27} = -2\)

\(h' = m\,h = -2 \times 7.0 = -14\) cm

**Nature.** The image is **real, inverted** (the negative \(h'\)) and **magnified** — 14 cm against an object of 7.0 cm, exactly twice the size.

The object at 27 cm lies between \(f = 18\) cm and \(2f = 36\) cm, which is precisely the range that gives a real, inverted, enlarged image beyond C.
groundedIn: §9.2.4 Mirror Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v + 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = -v/u\), with §9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors for the New Cartesian signs.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: Find the focal length of a lens of power – 2.0 D. What type of lens is this?
solution:
**Given.** \(P = -2.0\) D.

**Focal length.**

\(P = \dfrac{1}{f}\), so \(f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-2.0}\)

\(f = -0.5\) m \(= -50\) cm

**Type of lens.** The **negative** focal length identifies it as a **concave (diverging) lens**.

The sign is the answer to the second half of the question, so it must be carried through rather than dropped: “0.5 m” alone would describe a converging lens of the same strength.
groundedIn: §9.3.8 Power of a Lens, which gives \(P = 1/f\) with \(f\) in metres and makes the power of a diverging lens negative.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: A doctor has prescribed a corrective lens of power +1.5 D. Find the focal length of the lens. Is the prescribed lens diverging or converging?
solution:
**Given.** \(P = +1.5\) D.

**Focal length.**

\(f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

\(f = +0.67\) m \(= +67\) cm

**Type of lens.** The **positive** power and focal length identify it as a **converging (convex) lens**.

A converging lens is what corrects **hypermetropia**, or far-sightedness, where the image would otherwise form behind the retina.
groundedIn: §9.3.8 Power of a Lens, which gives \(P = 1/f\) in metres and makes the power of a converging lens positive, with §9.3.6 Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses.
